What is Paper Trading?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

DETAILED DEFINITION

Paper trading records hypothetical positions without exchanging securities or money. Simulators differ in source prices, fills and available orders. TradeHQ provides virtual funds and simulated market orders; it does not reproduce exchange queue priority, real slippage, limit-order execution, borrowing or brokerage settlement. Some quotes use dated provider observations, while other practice values or chart histories can be generated. For arithmetic practice, ten virtual shares purchased at $20 and later marked at $18 lose $20 in quoted value before modeled costs. Record both observation times and prices rather than treating that example as a measured investment result. Real account restrictions, taxes, liquidity and the consequences of losing actual savings are outside the simulation. No number of successful virtual transactions proves future returns or readiness for real investment.

HOW IT WORKS

Simulated trading with virtual money to study order mechanics and compare ideas. TradeHQ provides $100K virtual cash; practice outcomes do not predict real returns.

KEY POINTS
Simulated trades use virtual money; real trading can lose capital
Virtual practice illustrates mechanics but does not establish readiness for real capital
Limitation: doesn't replicate the emotional pressure of real trading
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Use virtual cash to study order mechanics and record assumptions. The experience differs from real liquidity, brokerage obligations and the consequences of losing actual savings.

Worked exercise and its limits

Buy 10 hypothetical units at $20 with a 0.1% fee: debit $200.20. Selling at $19 with the same fee credits $189.81, giving a $10.39 loss. Compare recorded fills with these assumptions; virtual results do not establish live returns.

References and scope
SEC Investor.gov — market, limit and stop order mechanics
